Paris Students Shut Down the Louvre
Artist Rosana Paulino makes a self-portrait of Brazil, protests in France and Colombia, and this month’s edition of Beer With a Painter.

“Brazil is a country that has never really looked at itself,” artist Rosana Paulino — one of the nation’s representatives at this year’s Venice Biennale — tells curator and researcher Daniela Mayer in an interview today. So Paulino sets herself to the task, coopting the European form of the illustrated naturalist album — “images made by foreigners for foreigners” — to represent the experience of Black Brazilian women.

All the world over, art is a flashpoint for political struggle. In Paris, art students block the entrance of the Louvre to protest France’s overcrowded and underresourced schools, Staff Repoter Anna Lee writes. In Colombia, artists are out on the streets, fighting back against the right-wing president's removal of artworks by women and LGBTQ+ artists from the national museum, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia reports. And a new film reviewed by Greta Rainbow laments Iranian authorities’ search and seizure of an archive lovingly assembled by painter and conceptual artist Nasser Bakhshi in Tabriz.

Confiscating, censoring, destroying — it’s the very antithesis of art, which safeguards memory, gives voice to the marginalized, builds something new. As Paulino puts it, “Fascism is against art, isn’t it?
—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor
Smiles Meyer Queers “The Last Supper”

For Smiles Meyer, art is an act of divine transformation — both creatively and bodily. In 2024, the Los Angeles-based trans photographer and musician staged “The First Gathering,” in which they recreated Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper” (1495–98) with trans models. Meyer is part of a growing tradition of queer and trans artists visualizing queer identities with longstanding religious imagery, with artists like Elizabeth Ohlson Wallin recreating scenes including the Last Supper. The series builds on their previous projects like the Mary + I cover and nightclub exorcism shots taken for performance artist Maris, allowing them to unpack religious trauma through art that explores and celebrates their gender identity. | Emma Cieslik
